parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A woman phones a council office to join the waiting list for an allotment (a small plot for growing vegetables).
script: Good afternoon, Calderbrook Council, allotments office. Greg speaking.
Oh, hello. I'd like to put my name down for an allotment, please. A neighbour told me there's a waiting list, but I'm not sure how it works.
That's right, there is. It's quite straightforward. I can take your details over the phone, and then we'll post you a form to sign. Could I start with your surname?
Almost. There's an H after the W. W-H-I-T-L-O-C-K.
Thanks, Ms Whitlock. And your address?
It's 31 Fennel Road, that's F-E-N-N-E-L, in the Eastfield area.
Fennel Road, lovely. We have to be sure you live in the borough, you see, because residents get priority. Could I have a contact number?
07712 903 468. Thank you. Now, we have three sites. Riverside is the biggest and the most popular, then there's Hollins Park, and Kiln Road, which is out by the ring road. Do you have a preference?
Riverside, definitely. It's only ten minutes' walk from my flat.
Ah. I should warn you that the Riverside list is very long at the moment. People are waiting about four years there. Hollins Park is much shorter, and Kiln Road is somewhere in between.
Four years! Goodness. Well, I don't want to wait that long. I'd better go for Hollins Park, then. I can get the bus there.
Hollins Park, fine. And what size of plot would you like? We offer full plots, which are about 250 square metres, or half plots.
Oh, a full plot sounds enormous. I work full-time, so I think I'd be overwhelmed. A half plot, please.
Very sensible. Most new tenants start with a half plot. A full plot costs 60 pounds a year, but a half plot is only 35 pounds, and the water is included.

Yes. And when a plot does become available, there's a refundable deposit for the gate key. It used to be 25 pounds, but it's been reduced. It's 20 pounds now, and you get it back when you hand the key in.
That's fine. Can you tell me roughly how long I'll have to wait?

At Hollins Park it's running at about 18 months at the moment. Last year it was nearer two years, but a few people have given up their plots, so the list has been moving faster. I can't promise anything, of course.
No, I understand. As long as I'm on the list.
Now, I have to ask, have you grown anything before? The site committee likes to know.
Only on my balcony. I tried herbs one year, basil and mint, but tomatoes were my real success. I had dozens of them last summer.

That's a good start. Tomatoes, on a balcony. I'll put that down. Right, the last thing is proof of address. We need a copy of a recent utility bill. I'm afraid we can't accept a bank statement any more, and a council tax letter doesn't count either, because it comes from us.
Right, so a gas or electricity bill. I've got one from last month.
That's perfect. Send it back with the form, and I'll make sure you're added to the Hollins Park list straight away. The form should arrive within three days.
Thank you so much, Greg. You've been really helpful.
You're welcome. Good luck with the waiting, and I hope you'll be growing your own vegetables before too long. Goodbye, Ms Whitlock.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: A park ranger briefs visitors at the start of the day in Larkmoor National Park.
script: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Larkmoor National Park. My name's Hana and I'm one of the rangers here. Before you set off, I'd like to spend a few minutes going through the things you need to know, so if you could gather round.

First, parking. Some of you will have seen that the car park at the north gate is closed. A lot of visitors assume that's because of the flooding we had last winter, but that was cleared up months ago. In fact, the surface is being relaid, and the work should be finished by the end of next month. Until then, please use the main car park beside this centre. There's also an overflow field just up the road, but it gets very muddy, so I'd avoid it if it's been raining.

Now, a word about dogs. You're welcome to bring them, and many people do. Between March and July, though, they must be on a lead on the open moor, because we have skylarks and curlews nesting on the ground there, and a dog running through the heather can destroy a nest without even noticing. On the woodland paths lower down, dogs can run free all year round, as long as they come back when called.

You might also be wondering about barbecues. Some websites still say you need a permit from the visitor centre. That was the old rule, and it no longer applies. What does apply is that fires and barbecues are allowed only in the two marked areas beside the lake. Anywhere else, and you risk starting a moor fire, which in a dry summer can be extremely serious. So please don't be tempted to light one in the woods, however careful you think you're being.

If you come across an injured animal, please don't try to pick it up or carry it to the visitor centre, however kind your intentions. A frightened animal can bite or scratch, and moving it often makes the injury worse. Instead, ring the park's wildlife line. The number's on the back of your map and on the board outside. Someone will be with you within the hour, usually less.

Now let me tell you a little about the places you're likely to visit. The most popular spot is Heron Pool, just ten minutes from here. A smooth, wide path runs all the way round it, so it's suitable for wheelchairs and pushchairs, and there are benches every fifty metres. You may spot herons, of course, but the kingfishers are more reliable early in the morning.

If you're feeling more energetic, you might try the Old Quarry path. The views down into the quarry are wonderful, but I have to warn you that the rock there is covered in moss, and after rain it's very slippery. Even in dry weather I'd recommend proper boots rather than trainers.

Beacon Hill is the highest point in the park. It's a steep climb and takes around ninety minutes, but on a clear day you can see all the way to the coast, forty kilometres away. Take a jacket, because it's always windy at the top.

Fern Gully is the little valley to the east of the lake. I'm afraid you won't be able to go there at the moment. It's closed until the end of May, because a pair of long-eared owls have nested there, and we don't want them disturbed. The signs are quite clear, so please respect them.

Finally, Miller's Bridge, a little way down the valley. If you'd like to see deer, that's the place. Wait there quietly around dusk, and you'll very likely see roe deer coming down to the stream to drink. Bring a torch for the walk back, though.

Last of all, we run a volunteer day on the first Saturday of every month. Last month we planted hedges, and this time we'll be repairing the paths that were damaged by the winter rain. No experience is necessary, we provide gloves and tools, and there's free soup at lunchtime. Just ask at the desk for details. Right, that's all from me. Enjoy your day, and stay safe.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: Two trainee teachers, Ellie and Daniel, plan the report they must write about a lesson they observed.
script: Right, Daniel, shall we go through our notes on Mr Brennan's lesson? Dr Patel wants the observation report by next week, and I'd like to have a plan before we both start writing.
Yes, good idea. I've got pages of scribbles, though, so I'm not sure they're in any kind of order.

Same here. Well, let's start with the beginning of the lesson. What I really liked was that the starter task was already up on the board when the students came in, so they sat down and got on with it straight away. Nobody had to be told.
That was good, yes. I was more struck by the way he greeted every student at the door by name. I thought that set a friendly tone. But I agree, the task on the board meant there was no wasted time.
And what about the boy who came in late? I thought Mr Brennan handled that really well.

He did. I expected him to make a fuss, or send the boy to the office, which is what happened in my placement school. But he just let him slip into an empty seat and had a quiet word with him at the end of the lesson.
Exactly. It didn't interrupt the others at all. Now, what about the group work? I know you had a few doubts.

Well, the task itself was fine, and the instructions were clear. It was quite noisy, but that's normal with Year 7. What bothered me was that in nearly every group there were one or two students who just sat there while the others did everything.
I noticed that too, though I'd say it was mostly the same couple of students. Maybe he should have chosen the groups himself instead of letting them pick their friends.
Possibly. Anyway, Dr Patel said we could choose one main area to analyse in depth, didn't she? Behaviour management, questioning technique or lesson timing.
That's right. I don't think timing gives us much to write about. He finished with two minutes to spare, and that was it.
And behaviour was hardly an issue. So that leaves questioning. He asked an enormous number of questions, and I thought the way he moved from simple ones to harder ones was really clever.
I agree, let's go for that. Did you manage to count them, using the chart she gave us?
I tried. My total came to 34, but I lost track in the middle when the groups were reporting back.
Funny, mine came to 41. So we'll need to explain that difference in the report, or the tutor will think one of us wasn't paying attention.
Good point. We can say we counted slightly different things. Right, shall we sketch out the sections?
Yes. Section 1 should just describe the class and the lesson. I think we ought to include the learning objectives, because the whole analysis depends on whether the questions helped to meet them.
Agreed. Then Section 2 is the main part, the types of question he used, open and closed. We can attach the tally chart at the end.
Good. For Section 3 we could cover the group work, and especially how he gave feedback. He used praise a lot, but I noticed he was also quite specific about what each group had done well.
Yes, that'll be a strong point. And Section 4 can be our recommendations. I'd suggest a visible timer for the group tasks, so the quieter students get a fair share of the time.
Good idea. Now, when's the deadline? I thought it was Tuesday.
That's the seminar. The report itself isn't due until Thursday, by five o'clock, so we do have a bit more time.
Phew. Then let's meet tomorrow to write the first draft.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecturer gives a talk on the science of bread and fermentation.
script: Good morning, everyone. Today I want to look at something that most of you will have eaten at breakfast, and that humans have been making for at least 6000 years: bread. Bread looks simple, but it is the product of some surprisingly sophisticated chemistry and biology, and I think understanding it makes you a better baker as well as a better scientist.

Let's begin with the flour. Wheat flour contains two proteins, called glutenin and gliadin. On their own they're not very interesting. But when water is added, they link together to form a network called gluten, and it's gluten that gives bread its structure. You can see this for yourself if you rinse a ball of dough under a tap. The starch washes away, and you're left with a rubbery, stretchy lump. That lump is gluten.

Now, kneading. Many people believe that kneading makes the dough tougher, but that's not quite right. What kneading really does is line up the gluten strands, so that the dough becomes more elastic. An elastic dough can stretch around the gas bubbles without tearing, and that gives a light loaf. This is also why wholemeal bread tends to be denser. Wholemeal flour contains sharp little particles of bran, and these cut through the gluten strands as you knead. The network is weaker, it traps less gas, and the loaf stays heavy, or rather, dense.

Temperature matters too. Bakers talk about the desired dough temperature, and for most loaves it's around 27 degrees Celsius. Some old recipes suggest 30, and you will get away with that, but the fermentation then proceeds so fast that the flavour has no time to develop. Warmer is not better.

Then there's salt. Most people think it's there just for taste, and it certainly does improve the flavour. But salt also tightens the gluten, which makes the dough stronger, and it slows down the yeast. Leave it out and the dough rises too quickly and then collapses.

Which brings me to the yeast. Yeast is a single-celled fungus, and what it does in dough is fermentation. It feeds on the sugars in the flour and produces two things: alcohol and carbon dioxide. The alcohol mostly evaporates in the oven. It's the carbon dioxide that matters, because it's trapped in the gluten network, forming bubbles and making the dough rise.

The first rise is called bulk fermentation. In the traditional method it lasted around 3 hours, but with modern, fast-acting yeast, 2 hours is normal, and that's what I'd suggest for the recipe in your practical notes. Some bakers prefer to leave the dough in a cold fridge overnight, which is slower but gives a deeper flavour.

Now, sourdough. This is bread made without commercial yeast. Instead, you use a starter, a mixture of flour and water that has been colonised by wild yeast and by bacteria. These bacteria produce lactic acid, and that's what gives sourdough its characteristic sharp taste. It's the same acid that you find in yoghurt, which is why some people find the flavours similar.

When the loaf goes into the oven, something dramatic happens in the first ten minutes. The heat makes the gas bubbles expand rapidly, and the loaf can grow by up to a third. Bakers call this oven spring. Eventually, the heat kills the yeast, and the crumb sets.

Finally, the crust. As the surface of the dough gets hotter than 140 degrees, sugars and proteins react to produce hundreds of different flavour compounds and that golden-brown colour. This is known as the Maillard reaction, named after the French chemist who first described it, Louis-Camille Maillard. That's M-A-I-L-L-A-R-D. It's not the same thing as caramelisation, although people often confuse the two.

So, to sum up: gluten gives the structure, yeast gives the gas, and heat gives the colour and flavour. In next week's practical session, you'll make three loaves, changing one variable each time, and you'll be asked to explain the results in terms of what we've covered today. Any questions before we move on?

passages.title: Ashgrove Business Park: staff parking permits
paras: From Monday 3 March, every vehicle parked in the staff car parks at Ashgrove Business Park must display a valid permit. The change follows complaints from tenants that visitors and delivery drivers were unable to find spaces.

Who can apply: Permits are available to anyone who works at the park for a tenant company. Each employee may have only one permit, although it can be used on up to two vehicles belonging to the same person. Contractors who work on site for more than four weeks may also apply, but they must provide a letter from their manager at the tenant company. Motorcycles do not need a permit, as they may use the designated bike bays by the main gate.

How to apply: Complete the online form on the park's website and upload a photograph of your vehicle registration document. Applications made before 14 February will be processed free of charge. After that date an administration fee of £10 will apply. Permits will be posted to your workplace within seven working days. The annual permit itself costs £120.
Visitors: Visitors should use the Zone C car park near the main entrance, where parking is free for up to three hours. Drivers must register their number plate at reception.
Penalties: A vehicle without a permit will receive a warning notice during the first week. After that, a penalty charge of £40 will be issued, which is reduced to £20 if it is paid within 14 days.

passages.title: Handling customer complaints: a guide for staff
paras: Hartwell and Pryce Building Supplies depends on its customers, and a customer who complains is giving us a chance to put something right. Handled well, a complaint can turn an unhappy customer into a loyal one. All staff who work with the public should follow the five steps below.

Step 1: Listen. Let the customer explain the problem in full. Avoid interrupting, even if you think you already know what they are going to say. Make brief notes, and repeat the main points back to show you have understood.

Step 2: Apologise. Say sorry for the inconvenience, whether or not the company was at fault. An apology is not an admission of blame; it simply shows that you take the customer's experience seriously.

Step 3: Record. Every complaint, including those made by telephone, must be entered on the Resolve system within 24 hours. Include the customer's name, the order number and a short description of what went wrong.

Step 4: Resolve. Where possible, solve the problem yourself. You may offer a refund or replacement worth up to £50 without asking anyone. For amounts above this, speak to your team leader, who can approve up to £200. Anything higher must go to the Complaints Manager.

Step 5: Follow up. Contact the customer within five working days, by telephone or email, to check that they are satisfied. If a complaint has not been settled within ten working days, pass it to the Complaints Manager, who will take over the case.

Customers who remain dissatisfied after eight weeks have the right to take their case to the independent ombudsman. Staff should explain this politely if a customer asks, and should never discourage anyone from doing so.

passages.title: Staff training programme: courses this term
paras: A  Effective Presentations. Two evening sessions, each lasting three hours. You will prepare a short talk and deliver it to the group, and your performance will be recorded on video so that you can review it with the trainer. Suitable for anyone who speaks to clients or colleagues.

B  Fire Marshal Training. A half-day session on Friday mornings. Compulsory for all floor wardens and recommended for anyone who works in the warehouse. Includes a practical demonstration of fire extinguishers.

C  Introduction to Spreadsheets. An online course which you can complete at your own speed, at work or at home, over a period of up to six weeks. No previous experience is needed. A certificate is sent by email on completion.
D  Managing Your Time. One full day, held on the first Friday of each month. Practical techniques for planning your week and dealing with interruptions. Places are limited to twelve.

E  First Aid at Work. Three consecutive days, leading to a qualification that remains valid for three years and must then be renewed. Includes practice in resuscitation. Staff who have completed the course in the past three years do not need to attend.

F  Leading a Team. Six weekly sessions of two hours. Open only to staff who have worked for the company for at least one year and who are, or are about to become, supervisors. Applications must be approved by your line manager.

passages.title: The story of the paperback
paras: A  Few objects are as ordinary as a paperback. It is light enough to slip into a coat pocket, cheap enough to leave on a train, and humble enough that nobody minds if the cover bends or the corners fray. It is easy to forget that this humble object once seemed a dangerous novelty. For most of the history of printing, books were expensive things, bought by the wealthy and kept for life. The cheap book that could be read, lent and discarded was a long time coming, and its arrival changed who read, what they read and where they did it.

B  Portable books were not, of course, invented in the twentieth century. Around 1501 the Venetian printer Aldus Manutius began to produce classical texts in a small format that could be carried in a saddlebag. His customers were scholars and gentlemen, however, and the books were still bound in leather and priced accordingly. A real step towards the mass market came in 1841, when a German publisher, Christian Bernhard Tauchnitz, started a series of English-language novels in paper covers. They were intended for British and American visitors to the Continent, who could buy them at railway stations and read them on the journey, and the publisher agreed that they would not be sold in Britain itself. Other firms followed, but their books were often badly printed on poor paper, and in the eyes of many readers a paper cover remained a sign of cheap, disposable reading.

C  The turning point is usually dated to 1935 and has become something of a legend. According to the story, a young publisher named Allen Lane was returning to London after a weekend in the country when he looked for something to read at the station bookstall and found only magazines and cheap thrillers. Good contemporary fiction was available only in hardback, at a price that put it beyond most people's reach. Lane concluded that there was an untapped market for well-made books costing no more than a packet of cigarettes. He launched Penguin Books with ten titles at sixpence each, and gave them simple, recognisable covers: orange for fiction, green for crime and dark blue for biography. Many traditional booksellers refused to stock them, convinced that nobody would buy a serious book for so little. It was the buyer for a large chain of department stores who placed the first big order, and the books were soon selling in thousands.

D  Lane's gamble worked because of simple arithmetic. A hardback publisher might print a few thousand copies, and each had to carry a large share of the costs of typesetting and design. By printing paperbacks in runs of tens of thousands, Lane spread those costs so widely that the price of each copy could be cut to a fraction of the hardback price, while still leaving a small profit. The sums only worked if the books sold in volume, which meant choosing titles with wide appeal and finding new places to sell them. Critics predicted that cheap books would cheapen literature. In fact the reverse happened: people who had never owned a book began to build small libraries, and the publisher's list grew to include history, science and poetry as well as novels.

E  A similar story unfolded in the United States, where in 1939 a New York firm called Pocket Books began selling small paperbacks at twenty-five cents. Its founders understood that the problem was not only price but also distribution. American bookshops were concentrated in a handful of large cities, and millions of people lived far from one. The new firm therefore sold its books at newsstands, in drugstores and at railway stations, wherever people already shopped for newspapers and cigarettes. Readers who would never have set foot in a bookshop now found novels beside the sweets and magazines.

F  War gave the paperback an unexpected boost. In Britain, paper was rationed and publishers had to use thinner paper and smaller type, yet demand rose, since books were one of the few entertainments that were never themselves rationed. In the United States, an organisation set up by publishers and librarians produced special editions for the armed forces from 1943. Printed sideways in two columns so that they fitted into a uniform pocket, more than a hundred million copies were distributed to soldiers and sailors, many of whom had rarely read for pleasure before. When they came home, a generation of new readers expected books to be cheap, and bought them.

G  After the war, the paperback gradually moved up-market. In the 1950s, glue replaced sewing as the usual method of binding, which lowered the cost of production again, and publishers began to issue serious non-fiction, textbooks and classic works in paper covers. University students, who had never been able to afford many hardbacks, became enthusiastic buyers. Some critics lamented the loss of the elegant hardback, but most readers did not mind. Today, sales of printed paperbacks face competition from electronic readers and audio books, yet the format has proved remarkably durable. Perhaps that is because the qualities that made it a success in 1935, lightness, low cost and a lack of preciousness, are exactly those that people still value in a book.

groups.instr: The text has seven paragraphs, A-G. Which paragraph contains the following information? Choose the correct letter, A-G.

items.q: a series of books aimed at foreign visitors
items.why: Paragraph B describes the Tauchnitz novels intended for British and American visitors to the Continent.

items.q: an explanation of how the price of each book could be lowered
items.why: Paragraph D explains that large print runs spread the costs.

items.q: an account of how a business idea began with a personal experience
items.why: Paragraph C tells the story of Lane's search for something to read at a station bookstall.

items.q: a description of books being supplied to members of the armed forces
items.why: Paragraph F describes the special editions printed for soldiers and sailors.

items.q: a reference to a change in the way books were made
items.why: Paragraph G says that glue replaced sewing in the 1950s.

items.why: Fiction was orange; crime was green and biography dark blue.

items.q: What does the writer say about the books of Aldus Manutius?
options: They were cheap enough for ordinary readers.
They were printed in paper covers.
They were sold at railway stations.
They were intended for educated readers.
items.why: His customers were scholars and gentlemen, and the books were leather-bound and expensive.

items.q: According to the writer, Lane could lower his prices because
options: authors accepted lower payments.
department stores paid in advance.
he printed very large quantities.
the paper was cheaper than for hardbacks.
items.why: Printing in runs of tens of thousands spread the fixed costs across many copies.

items.q: What does the writer say about Pocket Books in the United States?
options: Its books were sold in places where people already shopped.
Its books were mainly sold in large cities.
Its books were cheaper than those in Britain.
Its books were sold only by post.
items.why: Pocket Books used newsstands, drugstores and stations; the problem was that bookshops were in a few large cities.

items.q: What is the writer's view of the paperback today?
options: It has lost most of its readers to audio books.
It has become more elegant than the hardback.
It is still popular because of the qualities it began with.
It is no longer cheap enough to compete.
items.why: The last paragraph says the format is durable because lightness, low cost and lack of preciousness are still valued.

task1.prompt:
You have been offered a place on a short professional course that would help you in your job, but some of the classes take place during working hours.

Write a letter to your manager. In your letter:
- explain what the course is and why it would be useful in your work
- say exactly when you would need time off
- suggest how your work could be covered while you are away

Write at least 150 words. You do NOT need to write any addresses.

Begin your letter as follows:
Dear Ms Hartley,

task2.prompt:
More and more people are choosing to live in big cities rather than in small towns or the countryside.

What are the advantages and disadvantages of living in a big city?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.
